title: Survivor bias: why most business advice from successful founders is unreliable
summary: Jason Cohen argues that learning only from successes is a deep statistical trap. Using WWII bomber armor, the file-drawer effect, ESP experiments, and Good to Great, he shows how business advice may be luck dressed up as insight, and says to prefer advice that makes you think.

principles.text: Studying only successes systematically biases conclusions; the real data is in the failures you never see.
principles.quote: Planes with bullets in the cockpit or fuel tanks didn't make it home; the bullet holes in returning planes were "found" in places that were by definition relatively benign. The real data is in the planes that were shot down, not the ones that survived.

principles.text: Ask how many others did the same things and failed before crediting a famous winner's playbook.
principles.quote: what if twenty other coffee shops had the same ideas, same product, and same dedication as Starbucks, but failed? How does that affect what we can learn from Starbucks's success?

principles.text: With enough people trying, someone will hit improbable streaks by chance; picking the winner afterward proves nothing about skill.
principles.quote: The chance that somebody in a crowd of a thousand would flip heads ten times is a whopping 62%! Because so many people are attempting the feat, some normally-unlikely events will happen.

principles.text: A founder's own track record, including Cohen's, may just be the lucky one in the crowd, so past success doesn't guarantee the advice generalizes.
principles.quote: I've started three consecutive successful companies, so that's proof that I know what I'm doing and that you should do everything I say, right? Except maybe I'm just the one in the crowd who guessed right on the Zener cards three times

principles.text: Backward-looking business books that pick winners from a large pool may not predict future performance and ignore whether non-winners shared the same traits.
principles.quote: Jim started by combing through 1435 companies looking for good candidates for the book, and picked eleven. It's the ESP experiment all over again!

principles.text: You can't fully remove survivor bias from advice, but awareness helps; prefer advice that provokes thinking and builds on your own strengths over prescriptive answers.
principles.quote: prefer advice that makes you think rather than giving you answers, forces you to answer tough questions, and causes you to extend your existing strengths
